blocks.text: K. stared at the inspector. Was he being given schoolroom lessons here by a man who might be younger than himself? Was he being punished for his frankness with a reprimand? And was he to learn nothing about the reason for his arrest or about whoever had ordered it?

He grew somewhat agitated, walked up and down, which no one prevented him from doing, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed the three gentlemen, said, “It is quite senseless,” at which they turned towards him and regarded him with an obliging but serious air, and at last came to a halt again before the inspector’s table. “The public prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine,” he said, “may I telephone him?” “Certainly,” said the inspector, “but I do not know what purpose that would serve, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him.” “What purpose?” cried K., more dismayed than annoyed. “Who are you, then? You ask for a purpose and carry on in the most senseless fashion imaginable. Is it not enough to move a stone? These gentlemen first set upon me, and now they sit or stand about here and make me perform before you like a trained horse. What purpose would it serve to telephone a public prosecutor when I am supposedly under arrest? Very well, I shall not telephone.” “But do,” said the inspector, extending his hand towards the entrance hall, where the telephone stood, “please do telephone.” “No, I no longer wish to,” said K., and went to the window. Across the way the party was still at the window and seemed only now, since K. had stepped up to his window, to be a little disturbed in its tranquil watching. The old people were about to rise, but the man behind them reassured them. “There are more of these spectators over there,” K. called very loudly to the inspector, pointing outside with his forefinger. “Away from there,” he then shouted across. The three did at once retreat a few steps, the two old people even withdrawing behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, to judge by the movements of his mouth, said something unintelligible at that distance. But they did not disappear altogether, seeming instead to wait for the moment when they could approach the window again unobserved. “Intrusive, inconsiderate people!” said K., turning back into the room. The inspector possibly agreed with him, as K. thought he could tell from a sidelong glance. But it was just as possible that he had not listened at all, for he had pressed one hand firmly upon the table and seemed to be comparing the lengths of his fingers. The two guards sat on a trunk covered with an ornamental cloth and rubbed their knees. The three young men had put their hands on their hips and were looking aimlessly about. It was as quiet as in some forgotten office. “Well, gentlemen,” cried K., feeling for a moment as though he were carrying them all upon his shoulders, “to judge by your appearance, my affair would seem to be concluded. I am of the opinion that it would be best to give no further thought to whether your proceedings were justified or unjustified, and to bring the matter to an amicable conclusion by shaking hands. If you share my opinion, then, if you please”—and he stepped up to the inspector’s table and held out his hand. The inspector raised his eyes, bit his lips, and looked at K.’s outstretched hand; K. still believed that the inspector would take it. But instead he rose, took a hard, round hat which lay on Fräulein Bürstner’s bed, and carefully put it on with both hands, as one does when trying on a new hat. “How simple everything seems to you!” he said to K. as he did so, “we ought to bring the matter to an amicable conclusion, you were saying? No, no, that really will not do. By which, on the other hand, I certainly do not mean to say that you should despair. No, why should you? You are merely under arrest, nothing more. That was what I had to inform you of, I have done so, and I have also seen how you have taken it. That is enough for today, and we can take our leave, though only for the present. You will presumably wish to go to the bank now?” “To the bank?” asked K., “I thought I was under arrest.” K. asked with a certain defiance, for although his offered handshake had not been accepted, he felt increasingly independent of all these people, particularly since the inspector had risen. He was playing with them. He intended, if they should go away, to run after them as far as the front door and offer them his arrest. That was why he repeated: “How can I go to the bank when I am under arrest?” “Oh, I see,” said the inspector, who was already at the door, “you have misunderstood me. You are under arrest, certainly, but that is not to prevent you from attending to your profession. Nor are you to be hindered in your ordinary way of life.” “Then being under arrest is not so very bad,” said K., moving close to the inspector. “I never meant otherwise,” said the latter. “But in that case even informing me of the arrest seems scarcely to have been necessary,” said K., moving closer still. The others too had drawn nearer. They were all now gathered in a confined space by the door. “It was my duty,” said the inspector. “A foolish duty,” said K. unyieldingly. “Perhaps,” answered the inspector, “but let us not waste our time with such talk. I had assumed that you wished to go to the bank. Since you attend to every word, I shall add: I am not compelling you to go to the bank, I had merely assumed that you wished to. And to make this easier for you, and to make your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I have kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, here at your disposal.” “What?” cried K., staring at the three in astonishment. These pallid young men, so devoid of distinctive features, whom he still remembered only as a group beside the photographs, were in fact clerks from his bank, not colleagues, that was saying too much and already revealed a gap in the inspector’s omniscience, but subordinate clerks from the bank they certainly were. How could K. have overlooked this? How absorbed he must have been by the inspector and the guards, not to have recognised these three. The stiff Rabensteiner, swinging his hands, the fair-haired Kullich with his deep-set eyes, and Kaminer with his insufferable smile, caused by a chronic muscular strain, “Good morning!” said K. after a little while, and shook hands with the gentlemen, who bowed with due propriety. “I did not recognise you at all. Now we shall go to work, shall we not?” The gentlemen nodded eagerly and with laughter, as though they had been waiting for this all along, except that when K. missed his hat, which had been left in his room, they all ran one after another to fetch it, which did, after all, suggest a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors; the last was naturally the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had merely broken into an elegant trot. Kaminer handed him the hat, and K. had to tell himself expressly, as indeed he frequently had to do at the bank, that Kaminer’s smile was not intentional, that he could not, in fact, smile intentionally at all. In the entrance hall Frau Grubach, who looked by no means very conscience-stricken, then opened the flat door for the whole party, and K. looked down, as he so often did, at her apron string, which cut so needlessly deep into her massive body. Downstairs K., his watch in his hand, decided to take a motor-car, so as not needlessly to increase his lateness, which already amounted to half an hour. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the car, the other two were plainly trying to divert K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the doorway of the house opposite, where the tall man with the fair, pointed beard had just appeared and, at first a little embarrassed at showing himself now at his full height, stepped back to the wall and leaned against it. The old people were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for drawing attention to the man, whom he himself had seen before, whom indeed he had even been expecting. “Do not look over there,” he burst out, without noticing how extraordinary such a manner of speaking was when addressed to independent men. But no explanation was needed either, for just then the motor-car arrived, they took their seats and drove off. Then K. remembered that he had not noticed the departure of the inspector and the guards at all; the inspector had concealed the three clerks from him, and now the clerks in their turn had concealed the inspector. This showed little presence of mind, and K. resolved to observe himself more closely in this respect. Yet he still turned round involuntarily and leaned forward over the rear of the motor-car, in the hope of perhaps catching sight of the inspector and the guards. But he immediately turned back again and settled comfortably into the corner of the car without having made so much as an attempt to look for anyone. Although it did not appear so, he could just then have done with encouragement, but now the gentlemen seemed tired, Rabensteiner looked out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer was at his disposal with his grin, about which, unfortunately, humanity forbade one to make a joke.
